original_question: Over RCA0, are the following four statements equivalent: (A) the Halpern-Lauchli Theorem for any finite number of trees; (B) Milliken's Ramsey theorem for strong trees on one finitely branching infinite tree with no terminal nodes; (C) the canonical partition theorem for colorings of a fixed finite graph inside the Rado graph; and (D) the statement that for every k >= 2, the Rado graph has the rainbow Ramsey property for k-bounded colorings?
target_in_paper: Section 2, Problem (1), read together with the setup in Section 1 listing principles (A)–(D) and the known implication chain (A) ⇒ (B) ⇒ (C) ⇒ (D). The paper’s exact target is whether any of these principles are equivalent over RCA0, not whether all four are mutually equivalent. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1808.10227.pdf))
correct_elements: Your draft correctly identifies RCA0 as the base theory and accurately names the four principles from the paper’s setup: Halpern–Läuchli for any finite number of trees; Milliken’s Ramsey theorem for strong trees on one finitely branching infinite tree with no terminal nodes; the canonical partition theorem for a fixed finite graph in the Rado graph; and the rainbow Ramsey property for the Rado graph for each k ≥ 2. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1808.10227.pdf))
missing_details: The official problem in the paper is weaker than your draft: it asks whether any of (A)–(D) are equivalent over RCA0, rather than asserting or asking that all four are equivalent as a package. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1808.10227.pdf))

The nearby context records the already known ZF/ZFC implication chain (A) ⇒ (B) ⇒ (C) ⇒ (D), so the reverse-mathematical issue is whether any reverse implication holds over RCA0. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1808.10227.pdf))

Statement (D) is shorthand for a scheme quantified over every finite graph G and every k ≥ 2: if the copies of G in the Rado graph R are colored with countably many colors and each color is used at most k times, then some induced subgraph R' ≅ R makes all copies of G pairwise differently colored. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1808.10227.pdf))

Statement (C) is specifically the canonical partition theorem for colorings of a fixed finite graph inside the Rado graph; the paper only adds that this implies finite big Ramsey degrees, so it should not be replaced by that weaker consequence. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1808.10227.pdf))

The tree-theoretic ambient setting is infinite, finitely branching trees, and in (B) the paper explicitly requires one finitely branching infinite tree with no terminal nodes. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1808.10227.pdf))
refined_question: Over RCA0, which, if any, of the following principles are equivalent: (A) the Halpern–Läuchli Theorem for every finite number of finitely branching trees; (B) Milliken’s Ramsey theorem for strong trees on one finitely branching infinite tree with no terminal nodes; (C) Sauer’s canonical partition theorem for colorings of copies of a fixed finite graph inside the Rado graph; and (D) the statement that for every finite graph G and every k ≥ 2, every coloring of the copies of G in the Rado graph R into countably many colors, with each color used at most k times, admits an induced subgraph R' isomorphic to R in which no two copies of G have the same color? ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1808.10227.pdf))
justification: This draft is clearly aimed at the paper’s first numbered open problem. In Section 1 the paper introduces exactly the four principles (A)–(D) and records the known ZF/ZFC implications (A) ⇒ (B) ⇒ (C) ⇒ (D); immediately after that, Section 2, Problem (1), asks whether any of them are equivalent over RCA0. I therefore narrowed your question from the stronger all-four-equivalent version to the paper-faithful any-equivalence version, and I made (D) explicit using the definition of the rainbow Ramsey property given in Section 1. Also, this particular paper is only three pages long and does not contain a Conjecture 1.1, Proposition 1.2, or Theorem 1.3; the operative labels here are the Section 1 items (A)–(D) and Section 2, Problem (1). ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1808.10227.pdf))
